title: Reflexive Verbs
summary: Use reflexive pronouns when the subject acts on itself, as in se levantar and se chamar.

sections.heading: What reflexive verbs are
sections.body: Reflexive verbs use pronouns like **me**, **se**, and **nos** when the subject and object are the same person. In dictionaries they often appear with **-se**: levantar-se, chamar-se, sentir-se.

examples.en: We meet each other at work.

sections.heading: Pronoun placement in Brazil
sections.body: In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, the reflexive pronoun usually comes **before** the conjugated verb. With infinitives, it can come before the helper or attached to the infinitive.

examples.en: I am going to get ready now.
I am going to get ready now.

sections.heading: Common daily-routine verbs
sections.body: Many routine verbs are reflexive because you do the action to yourself. Some verbs can be reflexive or not depending on meaning.

examples.pt: Eu escovo os dentes depois do café.
examples.en: I brush my teeth after breakfast.
examples.note: often not reflexive in Brazilian Portuguese

keyPoints: Reflexive pronouns show that the subject acts on itself.
Use me, se, nos, se with eu, você/ele/ela, nós, vocês/eles/elas.
Brazilian speech normally places the pronoun before the verb.
Some English reflexive ideas are not reflexive in Portuguese, and vice versa.

commonMistakes.note: The attached form is formal; pre-verbal placement is natural in Brazil.
